summary: In Homer's Odyssey, Theoclymenus (Ancient Greek Θεοκλύμενος, "god-renowned") is an Argive prophet of the Melampodid line who flees after killing a kinsman, joins Telemachus at Pylos, and sails to Ithaca. There he reads bird-omens of Telemachus' house and Odysseus' presence, and at dinner sees a vision of the suitors' doom — which they mock until the slaughter that night.
etymology: Theoklúmenos combines theos ("god") and a fame/hearing root, yielding "god-renowned" or "famed by god" — apt for a seer whose visions the Ithacans refuse to credit.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Homer and the scholia make Theoclymenus son of Polypheides (and, in some notes, Aechme), brother of Harmonides, in the prophetic house that descends from Melampus. A minority tradition (Hyginus and others) links him instead to Thestor and thus to Calchas — a fork the atlas keeps secondary to the Odyssey genealogy.

sections.heading: In the Odyssey
paragraphs: Fleeing Argos after a kin-killing, he finds Telemachus at Pylos and begs a place on the ship returning to Ithaca. Telemachus takes him aboard. On Ithaca he interprets a hawk omen as a sign that Telemachus will head the royal house, and he tells Penelope that Odysseus is already home in disguise — she does not believe him.

At the suitors' feast he has a second sight of their death: the hall darkens, the walls drip blood, the guests' faces turn spectral. They laugh him out of the house; that night Odysseus and Telemachus kill them. Modern discussion sometimes links his solar imagery to a real eclipse over the Ionian Islands, but the poem's point is prophetic truth ignored.

sections.heading: Identity
paragraphs: The atlas id theoclymenus is the Odyssey seer. He is distinct from other Melampodids and from Calchas (calchas-thestor).
